The mainline walks the pipeline step by step, while the canvas arranges the same work as a node graph — both share one set of assets. macGatekeeper.question: macOS says the developer cannot be verified. Now what?
macGatekeeper.answer: Find DramaHub in Finder → Applications, Control-click the icon, choose Open, then confirm with Open in the dialog. You only do this once; after that it launches normally.

winSmartScreen.question: Windows says it protected my PC. Now what?
winSmartScreen.answer: Click More info, then Run anyway. SmartScreen blocks installers by default until they have enough downloads; it says nothing about whether this one is intact.

offline.question: Does the app still need an internet connection?
offline.answer: Yes. Script generation, first-frame rendering and video assembly all run on cloud compute; the app handles orchestration, media management and writing results to disk. Cuts already downloaded stay playable offline.

update.question: How do I upgrade?
update.answer: You don't have to. The app checks on launch, downloads new versions in the background and applies them next time it starts. To install a specific version by hand, see

storage.question: Where do projects and exports live?
storage.answer: Project data lives in the cloud with your account, so every device signed in sees the same episodes. Exported boards, first frames and finished cuts are written to local disk, and you can change that path in settings.

novelFormat.title: Premium drama format
novelFormat.intro: Premium drama scripts need explicit episode and scene boundaries. DramaHub splits the script by scene headers before generating visuals, dialogue, and audio line by line; it does not invent scene breaks for headerless prose.
novelFormat.standardStatusHint: Several industry formats are supported. Complete location, time, and INT/EXT metadata can be parsed reliably.
novelFormat.warningStatusHint: Scene boundaries are clear, but location, time, or INT/EXT metadata is incomplete and will be normalized.
novelFormat.blockingStatusHint: Import is blocked only when chapters are invalid or a premium drama has no recognizable scene headings.
novelFormat.repairableHint: The scene boundary below is recognizable but its time is missing. Import is allowed with a warning; the source is unchanged.
novelFormat.ruleEpisode: Start every episode with “Episode N”; list multiple episodes in order.
novelFormat.ruleScene: Give every scene its own header. Supported forms include “1-1 Location Day INT”, “1.1 Location INT Day”, split fields, and INT./EXT. headings.
novelFormat.ruleCharacters: Use “Characters:” for names of characters physically present in the scene, separated by commas; keep identity and performance notes out of this line.
novelFormat.ruleBody: Keep one visible action or shot per line; both “△” and “▲” action markers are supported. Do not combine several shots or speakers on one line.
novelFormat.ruleDialogue: Write dialogue as “Character: line”. Add a short performance cue in parentheses only when needed, and use “Character OS: line” for inner voice.
novelFormat.ruleLocationChange: Create a new scene header when the physical location changes. Both Location-Time-INT/EXT and Location-INT/EXT-Time orders are supported.
novelFormat.specTokenNote: The syntax labels (场次 / 地点 / 时间 / 内·外) and the Fountain format below are the required input tokens the parser matches — keep them as-is. Story content can be in any language, but scene headers must use these labels.

eighth.subtitle: DramaHub cares how a series keeps producing: text intake, character consistency, scene reuse, shot progression, team delivery.
eighth.title: Built for complete project planning

f1.answer: Ordinary tools work around one prompt, one clip, or one image. DramaHub targets the whole project: text import, asset accumulation, episode planning, shot production, and compositing export — a traceable, collaborative, reusable production loop.
f1.question: How is DramaHub different from ordinary AI video generation tools?

f10.answer: You land in the project management center. You can open an existing project or create a new one to start a new episode. Each project is its own space containing text, assets, episodes, shots, video, tasks, and composite results.
f10.question: Where do I land after logging in?

f2.answer: Follow the main workflow: import text in Story Source, confirm characters/scenes/props/voices in Asset Library, plan episodes and generate script and shots in Episode Studio, then export from the compositing page. The first goal isn't perfection — it's getting one episode all the way through.
f2.question: Where should I start on my first run?

f3.answer: Episode Studio is the main line — batch, stable, episode by episode. Freezone is the director's bench — refining key shots, exploring versions, finalizing assets, and handling complex video work. In a real project, ordinary shots go through Episode Studio and hard shots go to Freezone.
f3.question: What is Episode Studio for, and what is Freezone for?

f4.answer: No. Anything generated or uploaded in Freezone is a candidate by default. Results only enter the project's main line after you explicitly write them back and pick a target slot — character, scene, prop, beat sketch, first frame, or video.
f4.question: Do results in Freezone automatically overwrite main-line assets?

f5.answer: Rework in AI video usually doesn't come from the final generation step — it comes from unstable characters, vague scenes, unreferenced props, and inconsistent voices upstream. Asset Library turns those into assets first, which sharply reduces chaos in the later shot stage.
f5.question: Why organize characters, scenes, props, and voices first?

f6.answer: AI short dramas, comic-style series, novel promos, narrated shows, ads, and training video — plus team projects that maintain IP characters and serialized content long term. Solo creators use it to run the whole flow; teams use it to produce together.
f6.question: What content types is DramaHub good for?

f7.answer: Split by stage: the lead manages project, cost, and QA; the writer handles text and script; the artist maintains characters, scenes, and props; the storyboard artist or director owns shot expression; the video operator handles first frames, video, and compositing. Permissions map to viewer, editor, admin, and owner.
f7.question: How should a team divide the work?

f8.answer: First locate which stage is failing: is the text clear, is the character identity right, do scenes and props have references, does the sketch explain the shot, is the first frame stable, does the audio match? Don't start by regenerating video over and over — fix the upstream assets and shot descriptions first.
f8.question: What should I check first when generation is unstable?

f9.answer: DH isn't only short for DramaHub — it also stands for each creator's own content universe. DramaHub aims to help you start from one story and gradually build characters, a world, scene assets, and the capacity to produce serialized content.
